summary: Creates an IANA registry for SMTP enhanced mail system status codes, which RFC 3463 defined without a way to record new ones. The registry starts with codes from published standards-track documents and widely used industry codes. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Mail servers explain failures with number codes. This sets up an official list so new codes get recorded.

subtitle: An IANA registry so that new SMTP enhanced status codes stop colliding with each other.

tldr.problem: RFC 3463 defined enhanced mail system status codes and expected more to be added, but gave no way to register and track them, so conflicting definitions began to appear.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5248 creates the IANA registry "SMTP Enhanced Status Codes" with three tables, a Specification Required review model, and initial contents drawn from standards-track documents and a few codes common in the industry.
tldr.outcome: One place now records which code means what, which prevents collisions. The RFC is a Best Current Practice and updates RFC 3463, RFC 4468 and RFC 4954.

today: RFC 5248 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 138) published in June 2008. It updates RFC 3463, RFC 4468 and RFC 4954, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Registry Was Needed
sections.content:
Enhanced status codes for SMTP were first defined in RFC 1893, which was replaced by RFC 3463. That document anticipated that more codes would be added, but it provided no explicit mechanism for registering and tracking them.

Since then, various RFCs and Internet drafts defined extra codes. Without an IANA registry, conflicts in definitions had begun to appear. RFC 5248 defines the registry to help prevent further conflicts.
sections.eli5: People kept inventing new error numbers, and some used the same number for different things. An official list fixes that.

sections.title: Anatomy of an Enhanced Status Code
sections.content:
As specified in RFC 3463, an enhanced status code is a three-part numeric code with the parts separated by periods: the class sub-code, the subject sub-code and the detail sub-code.

RFC 5248 uses wildcards in its tables. An X stands for an unspecified class sub-code, XXX for an unspecified subject sub-code and YYY for an unspecified detail sub-code. So 3.XXX.YYY has an unspecified subject and detail, and X.5.0 has an unspecified class. This differs from RFC 3463, which used XXX for both the subject and detail wildcards.
sections.eli5: A code is like a street address with three parts: the big area, the street and the house number. The tables use letters when one part does not matter.

sections.title: The Registry and Its Entries
sections.content:
IANA created the registry "SMTP Enhanced Status Codes" with three tables:

  • Class Sub-Codes: entries with an unspecified subject and detail sub-code.
  • Subject Sub-Codes: entries with an unspecified class and detail sub-code.
  • Enumerated Status Codes: entries combining a specified subject sub-code and a specified detail sub-code, with an unspecified class sub-code.

Each entry records the Code, a summary or sample text, a description, a reference, the submitter and the change controller. Enumerated entries also record an Associated Basic Status Code: the basic SMTP reply code (from RFC 2821) it usually goes with, or a value such as "Any" or "Not given". That list is non-exclusive, and "Not given" entries can be filled in through updates to this document or at the direction of the IESG.

The reference should say whether the defining document is "(Standards track)", "(Best current practice)" or "(Not standards track)".
sections.eli5: There are three lists: one for big areas, one for topics, and one for exact codes. Each line says who wrote it down and what it means.

sections.title: Review and Updates
sections.content:
New entries are expected to follow the "Specification Required" model of RFC 5226, although in practice most entries are expected to come from standards-track documents. Non-standards-track documents that specify codes to be registered should be readily available. The principal purpose is to avoid confusion and conflicts among different definitions or uses of the same code.

Standards-track registrations may be updated if the relevant standards are updated. Non-standards-track entries may be updated by the listed change controller. Only the short description or references may change this way, not the code or associated text. In exceptional cases, any aspect of an entry may be updated at the direction of the IESG, for example to correct a conflict.
sections.eli5: To add a code, you must show a written description of it. Once a code is on the list, only small wording fixes are allowed, unless the top committee steps in.

sections.title: Initial Registry Contents
sections.content:
The class table starts with 2.XXX.YYY, 4.XXX.YYY and 5.XXX.YYY, and the subject table with X.0.YYY through X.7.YYY, all taken from RFC 3463.

The enumerated table is populated from sections 3.1 through 3.8 of RFC 3463, from X.1.9 in RFC 3886, from X.6.6 in RFC 4468 (but not its X.7.8), and from X.5.6, X.7.8, X.7.9, X.7.11 and X.7.12 in RFC 4954. Each source is a standards-track document, and each entry is change controlled by the IESG.

A table in the RFC gives the initial Associated Basic Status Codes. The RFC itself notes that this table is incomplete.
sections.eli5: The first version of the list was copied from earlier official documents, so nothing important started out missing.

sections.title: Three Codes Added by This RFC
sections.content:
Three codes that had been used in the industry without any published specification were registered directly, with RFC 5248 as the reference and the IESG as change controller.

  • X.7.10 "Encryption Needed": an external strong privacy layer is needed to use the requested authentication mechanism, mainly for clear text mechanisms. A client may activate a security layer such as TLS before authenticating, or try a stronger mechanism.
  • X.7.13 "User Account Disabled": returned after a successful authentication to a disabled account. The failure is permanent until the user contacts their administrator, unlike a generic authentication failure where a retyped passphrase might help.
  • X.7.14 "Trust relationship required": the submission server needs a configured trust relationship with a third-party server to access the message content. It replaces the prior use of X.7.8 for this condition, thereby updating RFC 4468.
sections.eli5: Three useful codes already in use, like "you need a secret tunnel first" or "your account is switched off", were officially written down.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As stated in RFC 1893, enhanced status codes may disclose more about how an internal mail system is implemented than the basic SMTP codes do.

Many proposed new codes are security related, and registering them in one place to prevent collisions improves their value. Security error responses can leak information to active attackers, for example the difference between "user not found" and "bad password". Documents defining security error codes should make clear when this is the case, so SMTP server software can restrict exposure.
sections.eli5: An error message can tell a sneaky person too much, like whether a username exists. Authors should warn about that.

items.label: Encryption Needed
items.desc: A strong privacy layer is needed for this authentication mechanism. Basic code 523.

items.label: User Account Disabled
items.desc: Authentication succeeded but the account is disabled. Basic code 525.

items.label: Trust relationship required
items.desc: Needs a trust relationship with a third-party server. Basic codes 535, 554.
